newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Hopes of Bangui unity government revive.
newsitem.headline: Hopes of Bangui unity government revive.

text.p: Efforts to form a broad-based government in Central African Republic appeared back on track on Friday after independence president David Dacko broke with hardline opposition allies and told his supporters to take part.

But it was not immediately clear whether President Ange-Felix Patasse and other hardline opponents would be able to bury their differences and form a unity government -- a key plank of an African mediated deal to end a cycle of political, military and ethnic violence.
"The political parties have resumed their discussions with the head of state and there is a possibility of forming a consensus government," Patasse spokesman Prospere Ndouba said.

Dacko said late on Thursday that his Movement for Democracy and Development (MDD) would join the government. "I told the MDD to join the government because the whole country is watching us," he told Reuters.
Patasse told representatives of the impoverished nation's 25 recognised political parties on Wednesday that the opposition had not responded to his outstretched hand.

"I do not want to go into the details of the consultations but before the Central African nation and international opinion I assume my responsibilities and the government will be formed shortly," he said.
Patasse named outgoing foreign minister Michel Gbezzera-Bria on January 30 to head the new government.
Joseph Bendounga, a leading member of the Democratic Council of Opposition Parties CODEPO alliance, said opposition hardliners wanted to exclude CODEPO from any government.

"That group wanted to grab all the ministeries and opposed the participation of CODEPO in the government," he said, adding his Democratic Movement for the Renewal and Evolution of the Central African Republic was prepared to join the government.

The January 25 Bangui Accord, brokered by Mali's widely respected former military leader Amadou Toumani Toure, was designed to end the country's third army mutiny in under a year and curb ethnic rivalry that had already led to bloodshed.

Troops from Mali, Burkina Faso, Gabon and Chad, whose presidents launched the mediation effort in December at the behest of a Franco-African summit, are taking over from French troops who have been keeping rival factions apart.
Troops from Senegal and Togo are also part of this force.
Mutinies in April and May began over pay and conditions but turned into a campaign to oust Patasse, a northern civilian who won presidential elections in 1993.
The latest mutiny, which began on November 15, degenerated into ethnic feuding. The mutineers were from the minority Yakoma tribe of former military leader Andre Kolingba, who replaced Dacko in 1981.
French troops, in the country under a defence pact, stepped in to restore order. Estimates of those killed in the mutinies range from scores to several hundred.

Jean-Bedel Bokassa, who later proclaimed himself emperor, toppled Dacko, his cousin, in 1966. A 1979 French-backed coup brought Dacko back to power, toppling Bokassa, whose cruel excesses brought the sleepy nation to the attention of the wider world.
